messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

David, a 33-year-old prosecutor from North America, has been grappling with symptoms following a traumatic experience of terrorism. His life took an unexpected turn when he was caught in the aftermath of a bombing that left several people injured and others dead. The event remains vividly etched in his memory, making it difficult for him to distinguish between what happened then and what is happening now. David often feels very tired or exhausted, which he attributes to the mental toll of reliving the trauma repeatedly. This fatigue serves as a trigger that heightens his emotional distress. He recalls the sound of an explosion one day while attending a professional conference, and it instantly transported him back to the scene of the bombing. The memory was so vivid and real that he felt like he was reliving the moment all over again. The trauma has left David with fragmented memories. When he tries to recount what happened during the attack, his mind goes blank or jumps between disconnected scenes. Despite this, the images in his mind are incredibly detailed and feel more real than memories of ordinary events. He often finds himself feeling as though the bombing is happening right now rather than something that occurred in the past. David’s inability to form a coherent narrative of what happened has led him to believe he will never forgive himself for not doing enough to prevent the tragedy. This belief is reinforced by his fragmented and vivid memories, which replay the events over and over again, each time with a different emphasis on his perceived failures. The more real these memories feel, the more David questions whether he could have acted differently or protected others. His feelings of guilt and inaction are compounded by a growing sense of distrust towards others. He feels that people are not what they seem, and this suspicion is only exacerbated when triggered by certain olfactory cues like the smell of alcohol, which reminds him of the chaos and confusion during the bombing. Every time he encounters these triggers, his negative appraisals intensify, making it increasingly difficult for him to trust those around him. David’s marriage has also been affected as a result of these symptoms. His wife has noticed changes in his behavior, such as increased irritability and withdrawal from social activities. He feels he is failing her by not being able to fully engage with everyday life or protect her the way he believes he should have protected others during the attack. The combination of guilt, distrust, and vivid memories keeps David trapped in a cycle where each component reinforces the other. His fragmented memories fuel his negative appraisals, which in turn make him more susceptible to triggers that heighten these emotions. He feels stuck and unable to break free from this cycle. David finally sought help after realizing how deeply his trauma was affecting his ability to perform at work and maintain a fulfilling relationship with his wife. What frightened him most was the possibility of being defined by this event, trapped in an endless loop of guilt and fear. He is hoping for relief from these symptoms so he can regain control over his life and reconnect with the world around him.
